title: API 510 Training in Newark: Pressure Vessel Exam Prep
description: Self-paced online API 510 exam prep for North Jersey vessel inspectors: Bayway refinery, Linden chemical plants and N.J.A.C. 12:90 owner-user programmes.
h1: API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Newark, Linden and the Arthur Kill Plants
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors in North Jersey

Newark's industrial shoreline runs south from Port Newark along Newark Bay, the Kill Van Kull and the Arthur Kill to Perth Amboy. The largest is the Bayway complex in Linden, where a refinery shares a fence line with an additive maker, an acid regeneration business, a cogeneration plant and a fuel terminal. New Jersey's own boiler and pressure vessel rules adopt API 510 by name.

Atlantis NDT's API 510 course prepares candidates for the API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector examination. It is self-paced and online: you enrol, start, and work through the Body of Knowledge at a pace that suits your shift pattern, and an instructor answers your questions from the code text. There is no Atlantis classroom in Newark. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification.

The Bayway refinery in Linden, read through EIA's figures

EIA's Refinery Capacity Report, which lists every operable US refinery as of 1 January 2026, shows Phillips 66 Company at Linden with 275,000 barrels per calendar day of operating crude distillation capacity, or 289,100 barrels per stream day. That is 275,000 of the 435,000 barrels per calendar day that EIA counts as operating in New Jersey. In barrels per stream day, the same table lists 75,000 of vacuum distillation, 140,000 of fresh feed to catalytic cracking, 39,600 of high-pressure catalytic reforming and 22,000 of solvent deasphalting, plus hydrotreating capacity for naphtha, gasoline and diesel.

Each of those lines stands for a family of vessels: crude and vacuum columns with their overhead accumulators and preheat exchangers; the cracking unit's reactor, regenerator, main fractionator and sour gas plant drums; reforming reactors and separators; deasphalting extractors and solvent drums; and hydrotreater reactors with their high-pressure and low-pressure separators.

Those services map neatly onto the RP 571 paragraphs the API 510 Body of Knowledge names for its current windows: sulfidation in hot crude, vacuum and cracking sections, naphthenic acid corrosion where the crude carries enough acid, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion and high-temperature hydrogen attack around hydroprocessing reactors, wet H2S damage in sour gas plant drums, hydrochloric acid corrosion in overhead systems, and amine stress corrosion cracking where amine treating is used.

The Environmental Protection Agency describes the Bayway property as roughly 1,300 acres holding a refinery, two chemical plants, tank fields and a distribution station; Phillips 66 has owned the refinery since 2012. The crude slate matters to a vessel inspector as well. OPIS reported in August 2026 that Phillips 66 was replacing Brent-linked crudes at Bayway with domestic US grades and expected to keep moving US crude there. A different crude changes sulfur, acid and chloride levels, and a change of service conditions is a standard reason to re-establish corrosion rates.

Steam, acid and additives: the rest of the Bayway complex

An economic impact study prepared by the New Jersey Institute of Technology for the New Jersey Business & Industry Association, built on 2023 data, names five firms in the Bayway Industrial Complex. Alongside the Phillips 66 refinery, with about 700 full-time workers and a polypropylene plant that Phillips 66 manages on site, it lists Infineum, which makes lubricant and fuel additives; Nexpera, which regenerates sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide and recovers sulfur gases; the Linden Cogeneration plant, a combined-cycle station of about 980 MW owned and operated by Linden Topco, LLC, which supplies steam to Phillips 66 and Infineum under long-term contracts; and a Sunoco LP fuel terminal.

That mix widens a vessel inspector's work beyond refinery hydrocarbons:

  • Steam and condensate. Imported steam ends up in flash drums, condensate receivers and deaerators, where boiler water and steam condensate corrosion, a Body of Knowledge paragraph, does its work.
  • Chemical and polymer equipment. Additive and polymer plants run stainless and alloy vessels beside carbon steel; read the chloride cracking and caustic paragraphs with them in mind.
  • Acid and alkali regeneration. Sulfuric acid corrosion matters in regeneration plants but is not on the current API 510 Body of Knowledge, so it is field knowledge rather than exam revision.

The cogeneration plant itself sits partly in a different jurisdiction. New Jersey's rules treat a heat-recovery steam generator as a boiler, covered by the boiler subchapter of N.J.A.C. 12:90, while the unfired vessels downstream of it fall under the pressure vessel subchapter.

What N.J.A.C. 12:90 asks of a New Jersey vessel inspector

The Mechanical Inspection Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance, part of the New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development, administers the state's Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Refrigeration Law and the rules at N.J.A.C. 12:90. Its own page puts unfired pressure vessels at roughly three for every boiler in the state. Four provisions matter most to an API 510 candidate:

  1. API 510 is adopted. N.J.A.C. 12:90-5.2 requires unfired pressure vessels to be constructed, installed, maintained, repaired and inspected to referenced standards, and paragraph (c) adopts the National Board Inspection Code and API 510, from the 1995 editions onward, as they apply.
  2. Who inspects. The Bureau carries out the inspection of new or replacement equipment itself; after that, the owner may choose a state inspector or an authorized insurance company inspector, or inspect through a registered owner-user agency.
  3. How often. Under N.J.A.C. 12:90-5.14, a vessel outside a registered owner-user agency gets a certificate inspection every three years after its initial inspection, while vessels under a registered owner-user agency are inspected at the intervals the National Board Inspection Code or API 510 requires.
  4. Owner-user agencies. N.J.A.C. 12:90-5.19 requires an owner-user agency that wants to carry out field inspection of unfired pressure vessels to register with the Bureau, beginning with a letter of intent, and to be audited at registration and every three years after. Its inspectors hold an owner-user Certificate of Competency, and each inspection record kept where the equipment is inspected must identify the inspector's National Board Commission or API certification number.

The rules define an owner-user agency as an owner-user of pressure vessels that maintains an established inspection department complying with National Board or API requirements. So the state adopts the code, and its records rule asks for the inspector's certification number. Pressurised storage meets a second state rule. At major facilities, the Department of Environmental Protection's discharge prevention rule, N.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16, sends pressurised steel tanks to API 510 or ASME Section VIII for integrity testing and does not allow API 510's similar-service or risk-based scheduling for them. None of these state provisions is examined; the API 510 test is about the code.

Worked example: the radiography marking that sets a drum's interval

The API 510 Body of Knowledge expects you to find the joint efficiency E from the nameplate's radiography marking (RT 1, RT 2 and so on), and it bases all static head on a specific gravity of 1.0, or 0.433 psi per foot. This example joins the two on an ordinary piece of plant equipment: a horizontal condensate drum.

Given: inside diameter 72 in, so R = 36 in; MAWP 150 psig at the top; liquid-full; allowable stress S = 20,000 psi at design temperature, as stated in the question; longitudinal seams are Type 1 double-welded butt joints; long-term corrosion rate 0.004 in per year; thinnest shell reading 0.420 in, on the bottom of the shell.

Step 1, pressure at the bottom. The liquid column is 6 ft, so the static head is 6 × 0.433 = 2.6 psi, and the design pressure at the bottom is 150 + 2.6 = 152.6 psi.

Step 2, the nameplate reads RT 3. Spot radiography gives E = 0.85 for a Type 1 joint. Circumferential stress governs: t = PR / (SE − 0.6P) = (152.6 × 36) / (20,000 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 152.6) = 5,493.6 / 16,908.4 = 0.325 in. The remaining life is (0.420 − 0.325) / 0.004 = 23.75 years. With no RBI assessment in play, the internal interval is the lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years: 10 years.

Step 3, the nameplate is unreadable and the data report is lost. With no evidence of radiography, the conservative assumption for the same joint is E = 0.70. Now t = 5,493.6 / (14,000 − 91.6) = 5,493.6 / 13,908.4 = 0.395 in, the remaining life is (0.420 − 0.395) / 0.004 = 6.25 years, and the interval falls to about 3.1 years.

Same steel, same readings, same corrosion rate, and the interval shrinks to roughly a third because a record went missing. That is the practical point behind the exam's joint-efficiency questions, and it is why New Jersey's requirement to keep a true record of every inspection at the site is worth far more than filing. In the exam, read the marking first, then choose the column of Table UW-12.

Routes into API 510 from Newark-area jobs

API counts education plus experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency, a term that includes the inspection department of an owner-user. The routes most often open to people already working around Newark Bay are these:

  • Engineering graduates. A BS such as the chemical engineering degree from New Jersey Institute of Technology's Newark College of Engineering needs one year of supervising or performing inspection activities as described in API 510.
  • NDT technicians. A UT, MT, PT or VT technician with a high school diploma needs three years in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels, including one year supervising or performing inspection. Thickness surveys and weld examination for an owner-user agency or an inspection contractor are the usual way in, and ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training for Newark candidates covers the method side.
  • Operators and maintenance staff. Time spent operating or repairing vessels counts toward the three-year route, but at least one year has to be inspection work, so an operator usually moves into the inspection group before applying.
  • Welders and boilermakers. Repair and alteration work counts; the inspection year decides the timing.

The New Jersey certificate of competency is a separate track. An owner-user inspector applies to the Bureau for it on the basis of experience and the certifications already held, while API 510 certification is decided by API alone, and holding one does not confer the other. The full eligibility rules are on the API 510 certification page.

Studying API 510 around North Jersey shifts and outages

Most candidates here study while working rotating shifts or a contractor's turnaround calendar, which is why the course has no timetable. A sequence that works with that kind of week:

  1. The code before the arithmetic. Read API 510 through, then the fifteen RP 571 paragraphs on the Body of Knowledge, then the recommended practices it lists. Ask the instructor while terms such as alteration and rerating are still new.
  2. Section VIII arithmetic. Shells and heads, static head, joint efficiency, MAWP, test pressure with temperature correction and fillet weld sizes at openings, practised until the steps are routine.
  3. Open-book searching. Timed searches in the ASME and API PDFs.
  4. Full papers. Timed practice exams that copy the closed-book morning and the open-book afternoon.

Outage calendars differ from site to site, so plan from your own schedule and the exam window you are aiming at rather than from a rule of thumb.

Preparation options around Newark, compared fairly

  • Classroom exam-prep courses run by training companies in the Northeast suit candidates who can be released from work for consecutive days; the cost is travel and lost shifts.
  • Employer programmes. Owner-user inspection departments and inspection contractors often mentor candidates and lend code copies.
  • University and college courses teach pressure vessel design and materials well, but they are not built around API's closed-book and open-book format.
  • Self-study costs least but leaves nobody to ask when a clause reads two ways.
  • Atlantis's self-paced course fits rotating shifts and turnaround work, with an instructor answering questions as you go; the trade-off is that you supply the discipline a timetable would otherwise impose.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a North Jersey plant or contractor

Registered owner-user agencies need enough qualified inspectors between triennial audits, and contractors serving Linden, Bayonne and Perth Amboy need certified people to sign reports. Employers can enrol several candidates on one quote, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API individually, with their own experience record, and sits the exam in the window they choose. Technicians not yet eligible can build their method qualifications first, and welding inspectors in the same group may also want the AWS CWI exam-prep course.

faq.q: Can I attend an API 510 class in person in Newark?
faq.a: No. The course is self-paced and online with instructor Q&A, and Atlantis has no classroom in Newark or anywhere else. You study at home or between shifts, send questions as they come up, and book the examination with API for a window that suits you. The exam itself is taken in person: Prometric lists test centres in and around Newark, and you choose one when you schedule.

faq.q: Does New Jersey require owner-user vessel inspectors to hold API 510 certification?
faq.a: The rules require owner-user inspectors to hold an owner-user Certificate of Competency from the Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance and to work for a registered owner-user agency, whose inspection department must comply with National Board or API requirements. Each inspection record must identify the inspector's National Board Commission or API certification number. API 510 is one recognised route, not the whole requirement. Read the current N.J.A.C. 12:90 text and ask the Bureau about your own situation.

faq.q: Are deaerators and condensate drums on cogeneration steam API 510 equipment?
faq.a: They are unfired pressure vessels, so they fall under the pressure vessel subchapter of N.J.A.C. 12:90, which adopts API 510 and the National Board Inspection Code. The heat-recovery steam generator that raises the steam is treated as a boiler under the boiler subchapter. For the exam, boiler water and steam condensate corrosion is one of the RP 571 paragraphs on the Body of Knowledge, so condensate equipment deserves careful study.

faq.q: I have a chemical engineering degree from NJIT. How soon can I sit API 510?
faq.a: With a BS in engineering or technology, API asks for one year of experience supervising or performing inspection activities as described in API 510, gained within the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. Process engineering on its own does not usually count as inspection experience, so many graduates join an owner-user inspection department or an inspection contractor first. You document the experience on the application and API verifies it.

faq.q: Does the API 510 exam ask about New Jersey's three-year certificate inspection?
faq.a: No. The examination covers the documents on the Body of Knowledge and effectivity sheet for your window: API 510, the listed RP 571 paragraphs and recommended practices, and the named ASME sections. State rules such as N.J.A.C. 12:90-5.14 decide how often vessels must be inspected in New Jersey, which matters at work but not in the exam room. Keep the two separate when you answer interval questions.

faq.q: Will a change of crude at Bayway change the corrosion rates I use?
faq.a: It can. Sulfur, acidity and chlorides differ from crude to crude, and they drive sulfidation, naphthenic acid corrosion and hydrochloric acid corrosion in hot sections and overheads. A change of service conditions is a standard reason to re-establish corrosion rates, and the exam tests how to choose between long-term and short-term rates. At work, the owner's corrosion and inspection staff decide which circuits need fresh readings.

faq.q: Should a Newark candidate take API 510 or API 570 first?
faq.a: Choose by the equipment you inspect most. Refinery and chemical plant inspection departments need both certificates, but a candidate whose experience is mainly columns, drums and exchangers will find API 510 the natural first step, while someone working dock, transfer and unit piping will reach API 570 eligibility sooner. Many inspectors add the second certificate later. See the API 570 exam-prep course for the piping side.
